title: L2 · NEWSROOM · The cost of money reset this week (rates, 22–24 Sep) · for marketing review
x:
The cost of money reset this week. Not in a headline. In a table the US Treasury publishes every afternoon.

Here is what it says, loan length by loan length. A thread.

Wednesday. Every loan length rose in one day.

The 2-year: 4.71% to 4.85%.
The 10-year: 4.96% to 5.11%.
The 30-year: 5.29% to 5.40%.

Where did it bite hardest? The middle.

The 3, 5 and 7-year each rose 16 basis points. More than the 2-year (+14). More than the 30-year (+11).

That middle stretch is where the market prices how many rate cuts are coming over the next few years.

So what got repriced on Wednesday was cheaper money. Not a recession. Different thing entirely.

Thursday it moved again, but differently.

The 10-year went to 5.18%. The 30-year to 5.47%. And the 2-year barely moved: 4.85% to 4.87%.

So the gap between the 2-year and the 10-year went from 26 basis points to 31 in a day.

Thursday was about the cost of lending for a long time. Not about what the central bank does next.

Why? On Thursday the US government borrowed for seven years at 5.085%. The highest it has paid on that loan since 1993.

And it had to pay slightly above what the market was quoting to get the sale done.

Indirect buyers, mostly foreign central banks, took 57.2% of that sale. Down from about 61% last month.

Not a failed auction. Buyers asking for a little more to lend for longer.

And shares? Flat.

S&P 500 on Thursday: -0.02%. Nasdaq: +0.01%. Borrowing costs at a 33-year high and the stock market shrugged. That tells you something too.

What it means if you hold good businesses for years: this reaches you through what companies pay to borrow, and what future profits are worth today. Slowly.

Not through one day's tape. I'm not alarmed. But I'm watching.

Every number in this thread is from the US Treasury's daily table and Thursday's auction results. Not advice.

Full edition, every source, on the BuyTrigger Newsroom.
